newsitem.title: USA: Airlines looking to fix jet fuel costs early in 97.
newsitem.headline: Airlines looking to fix jet fuel costs early in 97.

text.p: It's not even summer, but airlines already are laying strategies for winter jet fuel buying, especially after a painful season for many in the industry last year.

Jet fuel -- which accounts for 10 to 15 percent of a typical airline's operating costs -- is expected to be considerably cheaper this winter compared with 1996, when prices skyrocketed and caught most carriers unaware.

"We think jet fuel will be significantly lower in the fourth quarter compared to the runup last year and that is bound to help profitability," said David Swierenga, chief economist with the Air Transport Association, the airline industry trade group.

The higher '96 jet costs, which shot up 50 pct from July to October and remained high through the end of January, put a dampener on a cyclical upturn for the industry. Carriers intend to use their stronger financial position to take full advantage of lower jet prices this winter.
Airlines generally have been reluctant in the past to devote resources to hedging jet costs.

"Airlines have viewed hedging as a cost, and therefore, incremental in a business that has very high fixed costs, so to add yet another cost is something airlines have been very relutcant to do," said Vivian Lee, airlines analyst with BT Securities.
But they are coming round to the merits of hedging and at least three major airlines said that they are planning to hedge earlier this year and for a longer period than previously.
"We are talking about making swaps for the fourth quarter," said a fuel purchaser for one major airline who didn't want to be named.

"We are anticipating that prices will be better in the fourth quarter and yes we will look at locking in some fixed prices," said another executive at an airline which was hit by high fuel costs last year.
"As airlines are in relative prosperity, they have more time to focus on new hedging techniques," said Robin Wilson, a managing director of S H & E Inc, an airline consulting firm.
They are also aware of the happy experience of Continental Airlines last year, which presciently fixed the cost of its entire jet fuel needs through the winter before prices surged.

Houston-based Continental used options last year to fix prices and kept its jet costs significantly below the industry average. (Options give the right but not the obligation to either buy or sell at a certain price).
This year, Continental is scaling back on hedging in anticipation of lower jet prices.
"We expect to keep our option position to stay just at 90 days, unlike last year where at one point we were out almost nine months," said Larry Kellner, chief financial officer of Continental.
"We see less risk in the fuel outlook today than we saw a year ago," said Kellner.
